34.0: Yes, that one is their boat, Lily Briscoe decided, as she stood at the edge of the lawn. It was the boat with the grayish-brown sails; she watched it flatten itself on the water now and shoot away across the bay. He’s sitting there, she thought, and the children still haven’t said a word. And she couldn’t reach him either. The sympathy she had held back from him lay heavy on her. It made painting hard.
34.1: She had always found Mr. Ramsay difficult. Never once, she remembered, had she managed to praise him to his face. Because of that, what was between them had been reduced to something neutral, lacking the element of sex that made him behave so gallantly, almost gaily, toward Minta. For Minta he would pick a flower, or hand over his books. But could he really have believed Minta read them? She used to drag them all over the garden, with leaves stuck in them for bookmarks.
34.2: “Do you remember, Mr. Carmichael?” Lily was tempted to ask, glancing at the old man. But his hat was pulled halfway down over his forehead. He was sleeping, she supposed, or dreaming, or just lying there catching words.
34.3: “Do you remember?” she was tempted to ask him as she went past, her mind going back again to Mrs. Ramsay on the beach: the cask bobbing up and down, the pages flying. After all these years, why had that scene lasted? There it was, ringed round and lit up, visible down to the smallest detail, while everything before it was blank and everything after it was blank, for miles and miles.
34.4: “Is it a boat? Is it a cork?” Mrs. Ramsay would say—Lily repeated the words as she turned back to her canvas, reluctant once more. Thank heaven the problem of space was still there, she thought, and took up her brush again. It glared at her. The entire mass of the picture balanced on that weight. The surface ought to be beautiful and bright, feathery and fleeting, each color melting into the next like the colors on a butterfly’s wing; but underneath, the fabric had to be clamped together with iron bolts. It should be something your breath could ruffle, and something a team of horses couldn’t shift. She began laying on a red, then a gray, and began shaping her way into the hollow there. At the same moment she seemed to be sitting next to Mrs. Ramsay on the beach.
34.5: “Is it a boat? Is it a cask?” Mrs. Ramsay asked, and started hunting about for her glasses. Once she had found them, she sat without a word, gazing out to sea. And as Lily painted steadily on, she had the feeling that a door had opened: you walked through it and stood looking silently about you in a lofty place like a cathedral, very dark and very solemn. Shouts reached them from a far-off world. On the horizon, steamers disappeared into stalks of smoke. Charles was throwing stones and making them skip.
34.6: Mrs. Ramsay said nothing. Lily thought she was glad to rest in silence, not talking; to rest in the deep obscurity of human relationships. Who knows what we are? What we feel? Even in a moment of intimacy, who can say, This is knowledge? Mrs. Ramsay might have asked (this silence beside her seemed to have happened so often) whether saying things didn’t spoil them. Weren’t we more expressive this way? At least the moment seemed extraordinarily fertile. She jabbed a little hole in the sand and then covered it over, as though burying the moment’s perfection there. It was like a drop of silver: you dipped into it, and it lit up the darkness of the past.
34.7: Lily took a step back to put her canvas—so—into perspective. This business of painting was a strange road to walk. You went out and out, farther and farther, until at last you seemed to be standing on a narrow plank over the sea, entirely alone. As she dipped her brush into the blue, she dipped into the past there as well. Now Mrs. Ramsay stood up, she remembered. Time to go back to the house—time for lunch. They all walked up from the beach together, with Lily behind beside William Bankes, and Minta ahead of them with a hole in her stocking. How that small round hole showing her pink heel seemed to flaunt itself at them! And how William Bankes disapproved of it, though as far as she could remember he never said a word! To him it stood for the end of womanhood—for dirt and mess, for servants giving notice and beds still unmade at noon—everything he hated most. He had a habit of shuddering and spreading his fingers wide as if to hide something ugly, and he did it now, holding his hand up in front of him. Minta walked on ahead, and Paul must have met her, and the two of them went off into the garden.
34.8: The Rayleys, Lily Briscoe thought, as she squeezed out her tube of green. She gathered together what she knew of them. She saw their lives as a string of scenes. One took place on the staircase at dawn. Paul had come home early and gone to bed; Minta was out late. And there she was on the stairs at around three in the morning, wreathed, made up, garish. Paul came out in pajamas with a poker, in case it was burglars. Minta stood halfway up by a window eating a sandwich in the deathly early light, and there was a hole in the carpet. But what did they say to each other? Lily wondered, as if looking hard enough would let her hear. Something violent. While he talked, Minta kept on eating her sandwich, which was maddening. His words were indignant and jealous; he abused her in a mutter so the children wouldn’t wake—the two little boys. He looked withered and drawn; she looked flamboyant and careless. After the first year or so, things had come loose; the marriage had turned out rather badly.
34.9: And this, Lily thought, loading her brush with green—this inventing of scenes about people—is what we call “knowing” them, “thinking” of them, “being fond” of them! None of it was true, not a word; she had invented it. Yet it was how she knew them, all the same. She kept tunneling on into her picture, into the past.
34.10: Then there was the time Paul said he “played chess in coffeehouses.” On that remark too she had built an entire structure of imagination. She remembered picturing it even as he spoke: he telephoned home, the maid answered, “Mrs. Rayley’s out, sir,” and so he made up his mind not to go home either. She saw him in the corner of some dismal place where smoke clung to the red plush seats and the waitresses came to know your face, playing chess with a small man in the tea trade who lived at Surbiton—and that was all Paul knew about him. Then Minta was out when he got home, and after that came the scene on the stairs, when he fetched the poker in case of burglars (and no doubt to scare her as well) and spoke so bitterly, telling her she had ruined his life. Anyway, when Lily went down to visit them at a cottage near Rickmansworth, the strain was horrible. Paul led her down the garden to see the Belgian hares he bred, and Minta came after them, singing, and laid her bare arm on his shoulder so that he wouldn’t tell Lily anything.
34.11: Hares bored Minta, Lily thought. But Minta never gave herself away. She would never say a thing like that about chess in coffeehouses; she was much too self-aware, much too careful. Still, to go on with their story—by now the dangerous stage was behind them. Lily had stayed with them for a while last summer, and the car broke down, and Minta had to pass him his tools. He sat in the road fixing it, and the way she passed him the tools—businesslike, direct, friendly—was proof that all was well now. They were not “in love” anymore. No: he had taken up with another woman, a serious woman who wore her hair in a braid and carried a briefcase (Minta described her with gratitude, almost with admiration). She went to meetings and shared Paul’s views, which had grown more and more pronounced, on taxing land values and on a capital levy. That alliance, far from wrecking the marriage, had put it right. Clearly they were excellent friends, he sitting in the road and she handing him his tools.
34.12: So that was the Rayleys’ story, Lily thought, smiling. She pictured herself telling it to Mrs. Ramsay, who would be eager to hear how the Rayleys had turned out. There would be a little triumph in it for Lily, telling Mrs. Ramsay that the marriage had not succeeded.
34.13: But the dead, Lily thought—she had hit some snag in her design that made her stop and consider, stepping back a foot or so—oh, the dead! she murmured. You pitied them, you pushed them aside, you even felt a little contempt for them. They are at our mercy. Mrs. Ramsay has faded away and gone, she thought. We can overrule her wishes and improve away her narrow, old-fashioned ideas. She draws further and further away from us. Lily seemed to see her, mocking, at the far end of the corridor of years, saying the most unsuitable thing imaginable: “Marry, marry!” (sitting bolt upright early in the morning, as the birds began to chirp in the garden outside). And you would have to tell her, It has all gone against your wishes. They’re happy that way; I’m happy this way. Life has changed completely. At that, all of her, even her beauty, turned for a moment dusty and out of date. For a moment Lily, standing there with the sun hot on her back and the Rayleys summed up, triumphed over Mrs. Ramsay. Mrs. Ramsay would never know how Paul went to coffeehouses and kept a mistress; how he sat on the ground while Minta handed him his tools; how Lily stood here painting, and had never married—not even William Bankes.
34.14: It had been Mrs. Ramsay’s plan. Had she lived, she might have forced it to happen. Even that summer he was already “the kindest of men.” He was “the first scientist of his age, my husband says.” And he was “poor William—it makes me so unhappy, when I go to see him, to find nothing nice in his house—no one to arrange the flowers.” So the two of them were sent off on walks together, and Lily was told—with that slight touch of irony that let Mrs. Ramsay slip through your fingers—that she had a scientific mind, that she was fond of flowers, that she was so precise. Why this mania for marrying people off? Lily wondered, moving back and forth in front of her easel.
34.15: (All at once, as suddenly as a star slides down the sky, a reddish light seemed to blaze up in her mind; it covered Paul Rayley and poured out from him. It went up like a bonfire lit by savages on some faraway beach to mark a celebration. She heard it roar and crackle. For miles around, the whole sea ran red and gold. A smell like wine was mixed into it and went to her head, because she felt once more her own reckless longing to throw herself off the cliff and drown hunting for a pearl brooch on a beach. And the roar and crackle filled her with fear and disgust and drove her back. It was as if, even while she saw how splendid and powerful it was, she also saw how it fed on the treasure of the house, greedily and disgustingly, and she loathed it. Yet as a spectacle, as a glory, it outshone anything she had ever experienced; year after year it burned like a signal fire on a desert island at the sea’s edge, and you had only to say “in love” for Paul’s fire to leap up again at once, as it did now. Then it died down, and she said to herself with a laugh, “The Rayleys”—how Paul went to coffeehouses and played chess.)
34.16: Still, she thought, it had been a narrow escape. She had been looking at the tablecloth when it came to her in a flash that she would move the tree to the middle, and that she need never marry anyone, and she had felt tremendous exultation. She had felt she could stand up to Mrs. Ramsay now—which shows what astonishing power Mrs. Ramsay had over you. She said, Do this, and you did it. Even her shadow in the window with James carried authority. Lily remembered how it had shocked William Bankes that she disregarded the significance of mother and son. Didn’t she admire their beauty? he asked. But William had listened, she remembered, with his wise child’s eyes, as she explained that she meant no irreverence: a light here called for a shadow there, and so on. She had no wish to belittle a subject that Raphael, they both agreed, had painted divinely. She wasn’t cynical. Far from it. Because he had a scientific mind, he understood—proof of an unselfish intelligence that had pleased and comforted her enormously. So it was possible, then, to talk seriously to a man about painting. In fact, his friendship had been one of the pleasures of her life. She loved William Bankes.
34.17: They used to go to Hampton Court, and he always gave her plenty of time to wash her hands, like the perfect gentleman he was, while he wandered along the river. Their whole relationship was like that; a great deal went unsaid. Afterward they strolled through the courtyards and, summer after summer, admired the proportions and the flowers. As they walked he would tell her about perspective and architecture, and he would stop to look at a tree, or at the view across the lake, or to admire a child (his great sorrow was that he had no daughter). He did it in the vague, detached way natural to a man who spent so long in laboratories that the world dazzled him when he came out. So he walked slowly, lifted a hand to shade his eyes, and stopped with his head thrown back just to breathe the air. Then he would mention that his housekeeper was away on vacation and he needed to buy a new stair carpet. Would she perhaps come with him to buy a new stair carpet? And once, for some reason, the talk turned to the Ramsays, and he told her that when he first saw Mrs. Ramsay she was wearing a gray hat; she could not have been more than nineteen or twenty. She was astonishingly beautiful. He stood there gazing down the avenue at Hampton Court as though he could see her among the fountains.
34.18: Lily looked at the drawing-room step now. Through William’s eyes she saw the shape of a woman, quiet and peaceful, her eyes cast down. She sat lost in thought, pondering (she was wearing gray that day, Lily thought). Her gaze was lowered. She would never raise it. Yes, thought Lily, looking hard, I must have seen her look that way—but not in gray, and not so still, or so young, or so peaceful. The figure came easily enough. She was astonishingly beautiful, William said. But beauty wasn’t everything. Beauty had this price: it came too easily and too completely. It stopped life still—froze it. You forgot the small agitations: the flush, the paleness, some strange twist, some light or shadow that made the face unrecognizable for an instant and yet added something you saw in it ever after. It was simpler to smooth all that away beneath beauty. But what did she look like, Lily wondered, when she clapped her deerstalker hat on her head, or ran across the grass, or scolded Kennedy, the gardener? Who could tell her that? Who could help her?
34.19: Without meaning to, she had surfaced and found herself half out of the picture, gazing a little dazed, as if at things that weren’t real, at Mr. Carmichael. He was lying in his chair, hands clasped on top of his belly—not reading, not asleep, but basking like some creature stuffed full of existence. His book had dropped onto the grass.
34.20: She wanted to walk straight over and say, “Mr. Carmichael!” He would look up kindly, as he always did, out of his vague, smoky green eyes. But you only woke people when you knew what you wanted to tell them. And what she wanted to say was not one thing but everything. Small words that chopped the thought up into pieces said nothing at all. “About life, about death; about Mrs. Ramsay”—no, she thought, you could say nothing to anybody. The urgency of the moment always missed. Words fluttered off to the side and struck inches below the target. Then you gave up, and the idea sank back down, and you turned into what most middle-aged people become: cautious, secretive, with lines between the eyes and a look of permanent anxiety. Because how could you put these feelings of the body into words? How could you express that emptiness there? (She was looking at the drawing-room steps. They looked extraordinarily empty.) It was the body that felt it, not the mind. The physical sensations that came with the bare look of those steps had all at once turned extremely unpleasant. Wanting and not having sent a hardness, a hollowness, a strain right through her body. And then wanting and not having—wanting and wanting—how it wrung the heart, over and over! Oh, Mrs. Ramsay! she cried out without a sound, to that essence sitting by the boat, that abstraction made out of her, that woman in gray—as if to scold her for having gone, and then, having gone, for coming back. Thinking of her had seemed so safe. Ghost, air, nothing, something you could toy with easily and safely at any hour of the day or night—that was what she had been. And then suddenly she reached out her hand and wrung the heart like this. Suddenly the empty drawing-room steps, the frill of the chair inside, the puppy tumbling about on the terrace, the whole wave and whisper of the garden, turned into curves and arabesques flourishing around a center of total emptiness.
34.21: “What does it mean? How do you explain it all?” she wanted to ask, turning again to Mr. Carmichael. At this early hour of the morning the whole world seemed to have melted into a pool of thought, a deep basin of reality, and it was almost possible to imagine that if Mr. Carmichael spoke, a small tear would rip across the pool’s surface. And then what? Something would rise up out of it. A hand would push up; a blade would flash. Nonsense, of course.
34.22: She had an odd idea that he did hear, after all, the things she couldn’t say. He was an unreadable old man, with his yellow-stained beard and his poetry and his puzzles, sailing calmly through a world that met all his needs; it seemed to her that he had only to lower his hand where he lay on the lawn to fish up whatever he wanted. She looked at her picture. That, presumably, would have been his answer: how “you” and “I” and “she” pass and vanish; nothing lasts; everything changes; but not words, not paint. And yet it would be hung in the attics, she thought; it would be rolled up and tossed under a sofa. Even so, even of a picture like that, it was true. You could say of this scrawl—perhaps not of the actual picture, but of what it tried to do—that it “remained forever.” That was what she was going to say; or rather, since the words sounded too boastful even to her once spoken, she would hint it without words. But when she looked at the picture, she was surprised to find she couldn’t see it. A hot liquid filled her eyes (at first she didn’t think of tears); it left her lips firm, but it thickened the air and ran down her cheeks. In every other way she was in complete control of herself—oh yes! Was she crying for Mrs. Ramsay, then, without being aware of any unhappiness? She turned to old Mr. Carmichael again. What was it, then? What did it mean? Could things push their hands up and grab you? Could the blade cut, the fist clench? Was there no safety? No learning the world’s ways by heart? No guide, no refuge—was it all miracle, and leaping off the top of a tower into the air? Could it be that, even for older people, this was life?—startling, unexpected, unknown? For one moment she felt that if the two of them stood up, here and now on the lawn, and demanded an explanation—why was it so short, why so impossible to explain—and demanded it violently, the way two fully equipped human beings might speak who should have nothing hidden from them, then beauty would roll itself up; the space would fill; those empty flourishes would take shape; if they only shouted loudly enough, Mrs. Ramsay would come back. “Mrs. Ramsay!” she said out loud. “Mrs. Ramsay!” Tears were streaming down her face.

35.0: [To bait his hook, Macalister’s boy took one of the fish and cut a square of flesh from its side. Then the mutilated body (still alive) was tossed back into the sea.]

36.0: “Mrs. Ramsay!” Lily cried. “Mrs. Ramsay!” Nothing happened. The pain only grew. How anguish could reduce you to such a level of foolishness! she thought. At any rate the old man hadn’t heard her. He stayed kindly and calm—even sublime, if you wanted to see him that way. Thank heaven nobody had heard that humiliating cry of hers: stop, pain, stop! Clearly she hadn’t lost her mind. Nobody had watched her step off her narrow strip of board into the waters of annihilation. She was still just a skimpy old maid on the lawn with a paintbrush in her hand.
36.1: And now, little by little, the pain of wanting, and the bitter anger (at being called back just when she believed she would never grieve for Mrs. Ramsay again—had she missed her among the coffee cups at breakfast? Not at all), grew less. What their anguish left behind, as a remedy, was a relief that soothed in itself, and also, more mysteriously, a sense that someone was there—Mrs. Ramsay, freed for a moment of the weight the world had laid on her, lingering lightly beside Lily and then (for this was Mrs. Ramsay in all her beauty) lifting to her forehead a wreath of white flowers and going off with it. Lily squeezed her tubes again and attacked the problem of the hedge. It was odd how clearly she could see Mrs. Ramsay stepping, quick as always, across fields that were soft and purplish in their folds, full of flowers—hyacinths or lilies—among which she vanished. It was a trick of the painter’s eye. For days after hearing of her death, Lily had seen her like this, raising the wreath to her forehead and going off unquestioningly across the fields with her companion, a shadow. The sight, and the phrase, had power to comfort. Wherever she was—painting here in the country, or in London—the vision would come, and her eyes would half close, searching for something to rest the vision on. She would look down the railway carriage, or the bus; take a line from someone’s shoulder or cheek; look at the windows across the way; at Piccadilly strung with lamps at evening. All of it had been part of the fields of death. But there was always something—a face, perhaps, or a voice, or a newsboy calling _Standard, News_—that pushed through, snubbed her, woke her, and demanded, and in the end received, an effort of attention, so that the vision had to be made again and again. Now once more, driven by some instinctive need for distance and for blue, she gazed down at the bay, turning the blue bars of the waves into little hills and the more purple patches into stony fields. And once again, as always, something that didn’t belong startled her. In the middle of the bay was a brown speck. It was a boat—she saw that after a second. But whose? Mr. Ramsay’s, she answered. Mr. Ramsay: the man who had marched past her, aloof, with his hand raised, leading a procession, in those beautiful boots of his, asking for sympathy she had refused to give. By now the boat was halfway across the bay.
36.2: Apart from a streak of wind here and there, the morning was so fine that sea and sky seemed woven from a single fabric, as though sails were fixed high in the sky, or clouds had fallen into the sea. Far out, a steamer had drawn a huge scroll of smoke across the air, and it hung there, curling and circling ornamentally, as though the air were a delicate gauze that held things gently in its mesh and only rocked them softly this way and that. And, as sometimes happens in very fine weather, the cliffs seemed aware of the ships and the ships aware of the cliffs, as if they were passing some secret signal of their own between them. For though it was sometimes so near the shore, this morning in the haze the Lighthouse seemed immensely far away.
36.3: “Where are they now?” Lily wondered, gazing out to sea. Where was he—that very old man who had walked past her without a word, with a brown paper parcel under his arm? The boat had reached the middle of the bay.

37.0: They feel nothing over there, Cam thought, watching the shore, which rose and fell and grew steadily further off and more peaceful. Her hand drew a furrow through the sea, while her mind turned the green swirls and streaks into patterns. Numb and muffled, she wandered in her imagination through that underwater world where pearls clung in clusters to white branches of spray, where, in the green light, your whole mind was changed, and your body glowed half transparent inside a green cloak.
37.1: Then the swirl around her hand died away. The water stopped rushing past; the world was full of small creaks and squeaks. You could hear the waves breaking and lapping at the side of the boat as if they lay at anchor in a harbor. Everything drew very near. James had kept his eyes on the sail until it had become like a person he knew, and now it sagged completely, so they came to a halt, flapping about and waiting for a breeze in the hot sun, miles from land, miles from the Lighthouse. The whole world seemed to stand still. The Lighthouse stopped moving, and the line of the far shore stayed fixed. As the sun grew hotter, they all seemed to draw very close together and to sense one another’s presence, which they had nearly forgotten. Macalister’s fishing line dropped straight down into the water. But Mr. Ramsay kept reading, his legs tucked up under him.
37.2: The book he was reading was a small, glossy one, its covers speckled like a plover’s egg. Every now and then, as they drifted in that dreadful calm, he turned a page. To James it seemed that every page was turned with a particular gesture meant for him—sometimes assertive, sometimes commanding, sometimes designed to make people feel sorry for him. And the whole time his father was reading and turning those little pages one after another, James was dreading the moment he would look up and say something sharp to him about one thing or another. Why were they hanging about here? he would ask, or something just as unreasonable. And if he does, James thought, I’ll take a knife and strike him to the heart.
37.3: This old symbol—taking a knife and striking his father to the heart—he had always kept. Only now that he was older, as he sat glaring at his father in helpless fury, it was not the man himself he wanted to kill, not that old man reading. It was the thing that came down on him—perhaps without his knowing: that fierce, sudden harpy with black wings, its claws and beak all hard and cold, which struck and struck at you (he could feel that beak on his bare legs, where it had struck him as a child) and then flew off; and there he was again, an old man, very sad, reading his book. That was what he would kill; that was what he would strike to the heart. Whatever he did with his life—(and he felt he might do anything, as he looked at the Lighthouse and the distant shore)—whether he went into business or a bank, or became a lawyer, or ran some enterprise, that was what he would fight, what he would hunt down and stamp out: tyranny, despotism, as he called it—forcing people to do what they didn’t want to do, taking away their right to speak. How could any of them say, But I won’t, when he said, Come to the Lighthouse. Do this. Fetch me that. The black wings spread; the hard beak tore. And then, a moment later, there he was, sitting reading; and he might look up—you never could tell—perfectly reasonably. He might chat with the Macalisters. He might be pressing a gold coin into the hand of some freezing old woman in the street, James thought; he might be cheering at some fishermen’s sports day; he might be flinging his arms about in excitement. Or he might sit at the head of the table without a word from one end of dinner to the other. Yes, James thought, while the boat slapped and lazed about in the hot sun: there was a wasteland of snow and rock, very lonely and stern; and there, he had begun to feel quite often lately, whenever his father said something that took the others by surprise, were only two sets of footprints—his and his father’s. Only they knew each other. Then what was this terror, this hatred? He turned back among the many leaves the past had folded inside him, peering into the heart of that forest where light and shadow so dapple each other that every shape is warped, and you stumble along, now with the sun in your eyes, now in dark shade. He was searching for an image that would cool his feeling, set it apart, and round it off into something solid. Suppose, then, that when he was a child sitting helpless in his baby carriage, or on somebody’s lap, he had seen a cart crush someone’s foot, without meaning to, innocently? Suppose he had seen the foot first, smooth and whole in the grass; then the wheel; then that same foot, purple and crushed. But the wheel was innocent. And so now, when his father came striding down the hall early in the morning, banging on their doors to get them up to go to the Lighthouse, it came down over his foot, over Cam’s foot, over anyone’s foot. You just sat and watched.
37.4: But whose foot did he mean, and in what garden had it all happened? Because these scenes had their settings: trees growing there; flowers; a particular light; a few figures. Everything tended to arrange itself in a garden free of all this gloom and all this flinging about of hands, where people talked in ordinary voices. All day long they went in and out. An old woman was gossiping in the kitchen; the breeze sucked the blinds in and out; everything was blowing and growing. And at night a very thin yellow veil, like a vine leaf, would be drawn over all those plates and bowls and the tall, waving red and yellow flowers. At night things grew quieter and darker. But the leaf-like veil was so delicate that lamps lifted it and voices wrinkled it; through it he could make out a figure bending down, and hear some dress rustling, some chain jingling, as it came near and went away.
37.5: It was in this world that the wheel had passed over the person’s foot. Something, he remembered, hung over him and darkened; it wouldn’t move. Something was brandished in the air; something dry and sharp came down, even there, like a blade, like a curved sword, cutting through the leaves and flowers of even that happy world and making them wither and drop.
37.6: “It’s going to rain,” he remembered his father saying. “You won’t be able to go to the Lighthouse.”
37.7: In those days the Lighthouse had been a silvery, misty tower with a yellow eye that opened, suddenly and gently, in the evening. Now—
37.8: James looked at the Lighthouse. He could make out the whitewashed rocks and the tower, bare and upright. He could see it was banded in black and white; he could see its windows; he could even see laundry laid out to dry on the rocks. So that was the Lighthouse, was it?
37.9: No—the other one was the Lighthouse as well. Nothing was ever just one thing. The other one was the Lighthouse too. At times you could barely make it out across the bay. In the evenings you would look up and see the eye open and close, and the light seemed to reach all the way to them in that airy, sunlit garden where they were sitting.
37.10: But he caught himself. Whenever he said “they” or “a person” and began to hear someone rustling in or tinkling out, he grew intensely aware of whoever might be in the room. Now it was his father. The tension became unbearable. Any moment now, if no breeze came, his father would clap his book shut and say, “What’s the matter now? Why are we dawdling about here, eh?”—just as once before he had brought his blade down among them on the terrace, and she had gone rigid, and if an axe had been within reach, or a knife, or anything sharp, James would have grabbed it and stabbed his father through the heart. His mother had gone rigid all over; then her arm had loosened, so that he felt she was no longer listening to him, and somehow she had got up and gone off and left him there—helpless, absurd, sitting on the floor gripping a pair of scissors.
37.11: There wasn’t a breath of wind. Water chuckled and gurgled in the bottom of the boat, where three or four mackerel flapped their tails up and down in a puddle too shallow to cover them. Mr. Ramsay (James hardly dared glance at him) might wake up at any moment, close his book, and say something sharp. But for now he was reading, and so James went on thinking, stealthily, as if he were tiptoeing barefoot down the stairs, afraid a creaking board would wake a watchdog: what was she like, and where had she gone that day? He started following her from one room to the next, until at last they reached a room where, in a bluish light, as though reflected off a great many china dishes, she was talking to someone, and he listened. She was speaking to a servant, just saying whatever came into her mind. “We shall need a big dish tonight. Where is it—the blue dish?” Only she told the truth; only to her could he tell it. Perhaps that was the source of her endless attraction for him: she was someone you could say anything to, whatever came into your head. But the whole time he was thinking of her, he could feel his father following his thought, shadowing it, making it tremble and stumble.
37.12: In the end he stopped thinking. He just sat there in the sun, his hand on the tiller, staring at the Lighthouse, unable to move, unable to brush off these grains of misery that kept settling on his mind one by one. It was as if a rope held him there, a rope his father had knotted, and the only way to escape was to take a knife and plunge it in. … But just then the sail swung slowly round and slowly filled; the boat seemed to shake herself, then to move off, half conscious, still in her sleep; and then she woke up and shot through the waves. The relief was enormous. They all seemed to move apart again and relax, and the fishing lines stretched tight at a slant over the side. But his father did not stir. He simply lifted his right hand high in the air, mysteriously, and let it drop back onto his knee, as if he were conducting some secret symphony.

38.0: [The sea without a stain on it, Lily Briscoe thought, still standing there gazing out across the bay. The sea lies stretched like silk across the bay. Distance had an extraordinary power: they had been swallowed up by it, she felt; they were gone for good; they had become part of the nature of things. Everything was so calm, so quiet. The steamer itself had disappeared, but its great scroll of smoke still hung in the air, drooping mournfully like a flag in farewell.]
